media.title: A Hundred Lockers and a Queen's Will
media.context: This is the chapter opener and it plays before any objective. It covers the textbook's opening two puzzles and withholds everything that follows: no locker number is read out, no factor argument is made and neither squares nor cubes are characterised. Students arrive with factors and multiples from Class 7.
media.description: A hall contains one hundred closed lockers, and one hundred people walk past in turn. The first person flips every locker, the second flips every second locker, the third every third, and so on, with the hundredth person flipping only the hundredth locker. When the noise finally stops, only a scattered handful of lockers remain open—and their numbers are far from random. Elsewhere, a queen’s will divides land into a perfect square and a perfect cube, leaving the lawyers unable to agree.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Arouse curiosity about which numbers can be arranged into squares or stacked into cubes. Key teaching points: 1) A hundred flips leave only a few lockers open. 2) The open ones follow an obvious pattern. 3) A share of land can be square shaped or cube shaped. 4) Both puzzles ask what makes a number that shape. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often expect the open lockers to be random. 2) Students often think a perfect square is only about a shape, not about a number. Pause points: 0:30, at the end of a scattered handful: ask which lockers the class expects to stay open. 1:14, just before the opening question: ask what a perfect square number is. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask how many times locker twelve gets flipped. After viewing, ask what a cube of land would look like.
media.generation_prompt:
INTENT
Let two unrelated puzzles turn out to be asking the same question about a number's shape. Begin with the noisy locker process, end with a scattered handful of open lockers, then connect that curiosity to a queen's will involving a perfect square and a perfect cube. The film must open questions only and must not teach the answer, rule, factor argument, or later chapter content.

STORY
A hall contains one hundred closed lockers and one hundred people walking past in turn. The first person flips every locker, the second every second locker, the third every third, and so on to the hundredth. When the noise stops, only a scattered handful of lockers remain open, and their numbers are not random at all. Elsewhere, a queen's will divides land into a perfect square and a perfect cube, and the lawyers cannot agree whether the numbers she chose were possible. Both stories turn on the same underlying question about the shape of a number.

RENDERER
Manim Community Edition v0.18 or later. Scene subclass.
1920x1080, 16:9, 30 fps. Default frame is 14.22 x 8 units. All content inside a 4 percent safe margin. Nothing cropped.

CHAPTER VISUAL LANGUAGE, repeat verbatim in every video of this chapter
Background: dark slate #1F2937.
Primary object / first set: teal #0072B2.
Secondary object / second set: amber #E69F00.
Shared or agreeing: green #009E73.
Focus or highlight: reddish purple #CC79A7.
Neutral construction lines, axes, ticks: grey #6B7280.
Wrong, rejected or impossible case only: muted red #D55E00.
Text off white. Body 36 px equivalent, labels 28 px.
Prose uses Text. Mathematics uses MathTex with standard LaTeX only.
Flat fills, uniform line weights, no gradients or glow.

ASSETS
No external files. No image, SVG, font or audio imports. Build everything from Manim primitives: Line, Arc, Circle, Polygon, Dot, Arrow, Brace, NumberLine, Axes, Table, VGroup.

MATHEMATICAL TRUTH MODEL
Every value below is the only value that may appear on screen.

the hall: one hundred closed lockers
the visitors: one hundred people in turn, the first flipping every locker, the second every second, the third every third, on to the hundredth
what happens at the end: a scattered handful of lockers hang open
claim about them: their numbers are not random at all
the queen's will: divides land into a perfect square and a perfect cube
the dispute: the lawyers cannot agree whether the numbers she chose were possible
the shared question: what is special about a number that can be arranged into a square, or stacked into a solid cube

withheld:
which lockers stay open
the factor argument
the word factor
the exact pattern of the surviving locker numbers
every property, rule, formula, method or answer concerning squares and cubes
any worked solution
any later chapter result

ANIMATION RULES
Prefer animation over narration wherever a concept can be shown.
Every scene contains at least one transformation that carries meaning.
No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
Reveal progressively; never dump a finished diagram in one Create.
On-screen text minimal; no paragraph of prose on screen.
Objects that persist across scenes are transformed, never recreated.
No decorative-only animation.
The locker process should feel noisy and sequential at first, then settle into a quiet visual ending.
The queen's will should feel like a second, visually distinct puzzle, but the transition into the shared question must make the connection clear.
Do not reveal the exact surviving lockers or the mathematical pattern behind them.

MATHEMATICAL ACCURACY, highest priority
100 percent accurate to NCERT Ganita Prakash for Class 8. Correct notation, terminology, symbols and labels as used in the Class 8 textbook. Proportions true wherever proportion carries meaning; if a figure is not to scale it must say so on screen. No transformation may pass through a mathematically false intermediate state.

LANGUAGE
British spelling. No em dash and no en dash anywhere, in narration or on screen. Readable aloud by a student of this grade. Indian names and places for any person or setting.

NEGATIVE CONSTRAINTS
No value, label or claim absent from the truth model.
No rule, formula, method or answer from any later part of the chapter.
Nothing is taught here; the film only opens questions.
No text outside the safe margin, no overlapping labels.
No external assets, watermarks or branding.
No particles, sparkles or glow.
No answer to the locker puzzle.
No identification of the surviving locker numbers.
No use of the word factor.
No explanation of why the surviving lockers have their pattern.
No proof concerning perfect squares or perfect cubes.
No worked solution.
No additional numbers beyond the truth model.

SELF-CHECK BEFORE OUTPUT

1. Scene durations sum to exactly 90 seconds across 6 scenes.
2. Every number, count and label on screen appears in the truth model and nowhere else.
3. Every mobject named in a beat is declared in the inventory before it is used.
4. Every persisting mobject is transformed into its next form, never recreated.
5. No scene holds a static frame for more than 3 seconds.
6. All geometry lies within x in [-6.8, 6.8] and y in [-3.8, 3.8]; nothing is cropped.
7. No label overlaps another label; buff at least 0.2 everywhere.
8. British spelling throughout, and no em dash or en dash in narration or on screen.
9. Nothing in the film teaches a rule or reveals a later result.
10. The locker puzzle remains an open question rather than becoming a worked example.
11. The queen's puzzle remains an open question rather than becoming a worked example.
12. The connection between the two puzzles is curiosity about the same mathematical idea, not an explanation of that idea.
13. The film closes on curiosity about the chapter, not on an answer.

topics.summary: A locker is flipped once per factor, so most lockers close in pairs while square-numbered lockers, with their lone self-paired middle factor, keep an odd flip count and stay open.

content.text: Each locker is flipped once by every person whose number is a factor of the locker number, so the number of flips equals the number of factors. Factors usually come in different pairs, like 1 with 12 and 2 with 6 and 3 with 4 for the number 12, giving an even count, so the locker is flipped an even number of times and ends closed. A perfect square is different: it has one factor that multiplies by itself, such as 7 times 7 for 49, so that middle factor has no separate partner. This makes the number of factors odd, the locker is flipped an odd number of times, and it stays open. That is why exactly the square-numbered lockers finish open.

media.title: Square Builder
media.context: CBSE Class 8, A Square and A Cube, the opening of the square. NCERT Ganita Prakash builds squares on a DOT GRID and the older NCERT builds them as unit-square AREA; this tool reads the grid as unit tiles, which is legible in both. It sits BEFORE the square root is introduced in this same chapter, so the radical sign never appears and the reverse direction is asked as 'what is its side?', never as 'find the root'. Products are written with U+00D7. The chapter's own odd-number-sum pattern (1, 1+3, 1+3+5) IS the L-shaped border arithmetically, and the tool names them as the same fact.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the filled square or the rule test table that explains it.
whatYouLearned: A square of side n holds n times n tiles, written n squared
Squaring is not doubling; the two agree only at side 2
Stepping the side up by one adds 2n plus 1 tiles, so the growth is never fixed

overview.goal: The student predicts and then verifies the tile count of an n by n square, and writes n squared as a rule that survives testing at n equal to 5, 9 and 25.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground, the way squared paper sits on a desk, with the tile array as the only object on it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class argues that seven squared is fourteen, and the square itself is asked to settle it.
overview.concept: A square of side n is an n by n array of unit tiles, so it holds n times n tiles. That count is written n squared. Because the figure is a square, width always equals height, so one number n fixes the whole picture and the tile count follows from it.
overview.purpose: The student predicts and then verifies the tile count of an n by n square, and writes n squared as a rule that survives testing at n equal to 5, 9 and 25.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Square fills the main panel with the side readout above it and the tile count directly beneath. The n and n squared table sits to the right on a wide frame and collapses to a single scrolling strip under the square on a 390 px frame. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the tile count, the table or the rule while a prediction is still open. The count IS the answer.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Filling the square row by row gives n rows of n tiles, which is n added to itself n times, that is n times n. Stepping the side from n to n plus 1 adds an L shaped border of two arms of n and one corner tile, so the count grows by 2n plus 1 and never by a fixed amount, which is exactly why doubling cannot be the rule. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): A single tile is a legal square, and 1 is the one side whose count does not grow. Breaks: Believing a square must hold more than one tile before it counts as a square. ML2 (Medium, Edge Case): Doubling agrees with squaring at one side and nowhere else. Breaks: Squaring read as doubling, which survives precisely because side 2 keeps confirming it. ML3 (Medium, Edge Case): The doubling answer is not merely wrong, it is not drawable. Breaks: Squaring read as doubling, that is 7 squared taken as 14. ML4 (Hard, Edge Case): The rule outlives the picture. Breaks: Believing the count is always something you can get by counting. ML5 (Hard, Edge Case): Agreement at a single value is not a rule. Breaks: The empirical proof scheme: treating a few checked cases as a proof.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens on a 4 by 4 grid with the tile count HIDDEN and asks the class to predict how many small tiles a side of 7 will hold. Beat 2 fills the square one row at a time and the count lands beside the guess. Beat 3 steps the side up once and lights the added L shaped border in the second colour, so what each step adds is watchable before anyone writes a rule. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setSide, fillRows, highlightLShape and say. No drag: the agent cannot sweep a continuous control with finite calls.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the square at side 7 drawn as an empty outline with the count hidden, and ask the class to predict the tile count out loud. Commit the class number on the prediction pad. Target side 7. Never fill before the prediction is committed, and never say 49 at this call. Call 2. Fill the square row by row and let the true count land beside the committed guess. Point at the count readout. Target side 7, seven rows. Say what the gap between guess and count is, never whether the class was right or wrong. Call 3. Step the side from 7 to 8 and light the added L shaped border. Point at the two arms and then at the single corner tile. Targets side 8, and the border of 15. Read the added count from the tool's own readout, never from memory.

hunts: DOUBLING HUNT: find every side from 1 to 12 whose tile count is double the side, then say why the list cannot be longer.
L SHAPE HUNT: step the side up three times and name the size of each new border before it lights.
RULE BREAKER: find a rule that survives n equal to 5 and fails by n equal to 25.
BUILD YOUR OWN: set any side in range, predict the count, then let the tool check the prediction.

observationsAndConclusions.why: Each row holds n tiles because the figure is square, so width equals height
observationsAndConclusions.observe: The count climbs by a whole row each time a row lands, not by one tile
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: n squared is n groups of n, which is why it is a multiplication and not an addition

observationsAndConclusions.why: n times n equals 2 times n only when n is 2, so the two rules cross at exactly one point
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Side 2 is the one side where doubling gives the right answer
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: A rule that is right once is not right; agreement at one value proves nothing

observationsAndConclusions.why: The outer square minus the inner square is 2n plus 1 tiles
observationsAndConclusions.observe: Stepping the side up adds an L of two arms and one corner
observationsAndConclusions.conclusion: The step grows with n, so the count cannot be produced by doubling anything

media.description: A square of unit tiles stands on a plain working ground with one drag handle that moves its width and its height together, so a single number n fixes the whole picture. The array fills one row at a time from the bottom, the count climbing by a whole row rather than by a tile, and a running table of n against n squared builds beside it on a wide pane. Stepping the side up by one lights the added L shaped border in a second colour, drawn as three separately counted pieces - an arm of n, a second arm of n, and one corner tile that lands last - so 2n + 1 is watched rather than asserted, and the same number is named as the next odd number, which is the textbook's own explanation of the growth. A claimed count that cannot be a square is drawn as tiles that RUN OUT inside the ruled grid, with a bracket strip placing it between the two whole sides that bracket it, so the doubling error is refuted by a picture of an unfinishable square rather than by a red cross. Above side 12 the tiles stop being drawn and the square becomes a labelled outline carrying its count, which is where the rule has to take over from counting. A typed rule is parsed to a small expression tree - never eval - and run against the tool's own ground truth at n equal to 5, 9 and 25, with every disagreeing row washed in the second colour, because agreement at a single value is not a rule.

Beat 3 steps the side up once and lights the added L shaped border in the second colour, so what each step adds is watchable before anyone writes a rule. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setSide, fillRows, highlightLShape and say. No drag: the agent cannot sweep a continuous control with finite calls.
mods.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own square. Give the tile count for a stated side, give the side for a stated count, or type a rule for any side n. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer and the square that settles it.
mods.free_play: Free Play, student operated. The student drags the side from 1 to 12, fills and empties the square, shows or hides the n and n squared table, and tests any rule they like against fresh values of n. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.

whatYouLearned: A square of side n holds n times n tiles, written n squared
Squaring is not doubling; the two agree only at side 2
Stepping the side up by one adds 2n plus 1 tiles, so the growth is never fixed

concept.notation: Write n squared, read as 'n squared' or 'n to the power 2'. The raised 2 counts how many factors of n are multiplied, it is not a multiplier.
concept.statement: A square of side n is an n by n array of unit tiles, so it holds n times n tiles. That count is written n squared. Because the figure is a square, width always equals height, so one number n fixes the whole picture and the tile count follows from it.
prerequisites: area of a rectangle as length times breadth from Class 7
misconceptions: Squaring read as doubling, so 7 squared is taken as 14. The array makes 14 impossible to draw as a square.
Reading the raised 2 as 'times 2' rather than as a count of equal factors.
concept.why_it_is_true: Filling the square row by row gives n rows of n tiles, which is n added to itself n times, that is n times n. Stepping the side from n to n plus 1 adds an L shaped border of two arms of n and one corner tile, so the count grows by 2n plus 1 and never by a fixed amount, which is exactly why doubling cannot be the rule.
worked_numbers: side 4 gives 4 rows of 4, so 16 tiles; doubling would have said 8.
side 7 gives 49 tiles; the doubling answer 14 is smaller than one row of the square plus its neighbour.
side 12 gives 144 tiles, the largest square the grid draws before it switches to an outline.

answer_key.worked: A square of side n holds n times n tiles, written n squared. The count is the area of the square in unit tiles.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn square: the tile count for the stated side, the side for the stated count, or whether the typed rule agrees with n squared at every tested n.
answer_key.precision: Integer arithmetic only. No floating point value decides a tile count or a side, and no rule is graded by string comparison.
answer_key.ground_truth: tiles(n) = n * n, computed as an integer product. side(t) = the integer s with s*s === t, found by integer search, or null when no such s exists. ruleAgrees(text) = parse the typed rule to a small expression tree and evaluate it at n = 5, 9 and 25, comparing each value with n*n.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: A single tile. It is a legal square and the smallest one, and the table starts at 1 and 1 so the student sees that squaring leaves 1 unmoved. Never treat it as an empty scene.

edge_cases.case: A tile count that is not a perfect square
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The tool refuses to draw it as a square and says why, showing the two whole sides it falls between. It never rounds a side to make the picture work.
The grid is drawn as an outline with the side labelled and no individual tiles, so counting is impossible and the rule has to be used. The tool says on screen that the tiles are not drawn.

edge_cases.case: A rule that happens to agree at one n
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: Agreement at a single value never closes the stage. The rule is run at n equal to 5, 9 and 25 and the first row that disagrees is named, because one case is not a proof.

edge_cases.case: A prediction typed before any side is chosen
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The prediction box stays locked until a side is set, so a guess is always a guess about a stated square rather than about nothing.

questions.description: Replaces the built in practice bank. Items are {kind:'count_tiles', n:number} | {kind:'find_side', tiles:number} | {kind:'state_rule', testAt:number[]} | {kind:'choice', prompt, options[], correct, explain}.

showTable.description: Show the running table of n against n squared beside the square. Hidden in Stage 3 so the rule has to be used rather than read off.

startingSide.description: The side the square opens on, clamped 1 to 12.

constraints: The figure stays a square at every moment: width always equals height, and a drag that would separate them is refused rather than corrected silently.
Tiles stay whole and non overlapping. No partial tile is ever drawn to make a count come out.
The tile count is computed as an integer product n * n, never accumulated by counting rendered rects, so a redraw cannot drift.
Render is capped at 144 tiles. Above a side of 12 the square switches to a labelled outline and the tool says the tiles are not drawn.
A typed rule is parsed to a small expression tree and evaluated numerically, never passed to eval, so 2n plus 1 style input is safe and n times n and n squared both pass.

extra.concept_only: Concept carries no questions of its own. Its beats reveal the idea and then run one reasoning beat each, and every number the agent says is read from state.truth.

ai.shows: The square, the teacher caption, the prediction pad, and discrete step navigation (Prev / Step k of 3 / Next) with a progress bar.
steps: Predict: the grid is drawn at side 7 as an empty outline with the count hidden. The class commits a tile count out loud and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.

Step: the side moves from 7 to 8 and the added L shaped border lights in the second colour, two arms of 7 and one corner, so the step of 15 is seen rather than stated.

play_modes: DOUBLING HUNT: find every side from 1 to 12 whose tile count is double the side, then say why the list cannot be longer.
L SHAPE HUNT: step the side up three times and name the size of each new border before it lights.
RULE BREAKER: find a rule that survives n equal to 5 and fails by n equal to 25.
BUILD YOUR OWN: set any side in range, predict the count, then let the tool check the prediction.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. The hunts below are starting points, not a syllabus.

shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example setting the side a child names and filling it row by row to settle an argument.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists so the count is SEEN arriving as seven groups of seven rather than as a block appearing. The array fills a row at a time and the count climbs by a whole row, which is what makes n squared a multiplication instead of an addition. Do not write the rule down at this beat; it is the count that is being made.

Beat 2 is the refutation, and it works because 14 is EXACTLY two rows of seven. The fourteen tiles fill two complete rows and then stop, with five rows of the ruled grid still empty, so the doubling answer is not merely wrong on paper - it is an unfinishable square. The bracket strip then shows 14 sitting between 9 and 16, which is why no whole side gives it at all.

Beat 3 turns the observation into a rule the class can test. The added border arrives as three separately counted pieces and the corner tile lands LAST, so a student who said '+1' watches fifteen tiles land and a student who said '+7' sees the second arm and the corner arrive after their answer was complete. The second chip carries 9 to 10 adding 19, because one step teaches nothing here and two do: the step GROWS, which is precisely why doubling cannot be the rule.

media.title: Tiles That Snap Into a Square
media.context: This hook opens the topic on squares as area and on their digits. Students know that squares have an odd factor count. The film must not list the possible last digits and must not state the trailing zero rule.
media.description: Tip a box of square tiles onto the desk and try to arrange them into a perfect square with no gaps and no leftovers. Nine tiles snap into a neat three by three, ten leave one stranded. Some counts fit exactly and some never will.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: See that a perfect square is the area of a square array, and that its last digit can rule it out. Key teaching points: 1) A number of tiles forms a square only if it is a side length multiplied by itself. 2) That number is called a perfect square. 3) A square can only end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. 4) A last digit can reject a number but can never confirm it. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often think any last digit test can prove a number is a square. 2) Students often forget that one is itself a perfect square. Pause points: 0:24, at the end of some never will: ask how many tiles the next perfect square needs. 0:24, just before the open question: ask which last digits the class has seen on squares. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask whether a number ending in seven could be a square. After viewing, ask what makes a count of tiles fit exactly.

topics.summary: n squared is the area of an n by n grid, so the perfect squares are exactly the numbers that fill a full square. Their units digit can only rule a square out, their trailing zeros come in even counts, and a square keeps the parity of its number.

content.text: The number of unit squares in a square is its area, which is the side times the side. So a square of side n has area n times n, written n squared and read n squared. The numbers you get this way, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and so on, are called perfect squares because each one fills a complete square grid with nothing left over. To test whether a number is a perfect square, try to lay it out as a full n by n grid: if it closes exactly, the number is a perfect square and n is the side of the grid.

content.text: Every perfect square ends in one of the digits 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. It never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8. So if a number ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8, you can be sure at once that it is not a perfect square, with no calculation at all. But the reverse is not true. Plenty of numbers that end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 are not squares, such as 66, 91 or 120. So a good last digit keeps a number possible, but it does not prove the number is a square. The units digit is a quick way to reject a number, never a way to confirm one.

content.text: When you square a number, every trailing zero is doubled, because each ending zero comes from a factor of ten and squaring makes each factor appear twice. So a number ending in one zero gives a square ending in two zeros, two zeros give four, and so on. This means a perfect square always ends in an even number of zeros, and a number ending in an odd number of zeros, like three or five, can never be a perfect square. Squaring also keeps the number's parity: an even number squared is even, and an odd number squared is odd.

The numbers you get this way, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25 and so on, are called perfect squares because each one fills a complete square grid with nothing left over. To test whether a number is a perfect square, try to lay it out as a full n by n grid: if it closes exactly, the number is a perfect square and n is the side of the grid. Every perfect square ends in one of the digits 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9. It never ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8. So if a number ends in 2, 3, 7 or 8, you can be sure at once that it is not a perfect square, with no calculation at all. But the reverse is not true. Plenty of numbers that end in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 are not squares, such as 66, 91 or 120. So a good last digit keeps a number possible, but it does not prove the number is a square. learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the count of unit squares in a grid represents through observation and reasoning, and determine that a square of side n holds n times n unit squares, so n squared equals the area of that square and the numbers 1, 4, 9, 16 formed this way are perfect squares. They will explain that a number is a perfect square exactly when it can be laid out as a full n by n grid that closes with nothing left over, and then n is its side.

Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving n squared is the area of an n by n square, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what the final digit of a number tells them through observation and reasoning, and determine that every perfect square ends in 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 and never in 2, 3, 7 or 8. They will explain that a final digit of 2, 3, 7 or 8 rejects a number at once, while a final digit of 0, 1, 4, 5, 6 or 9 only keeps it possible and never confirms it, since 66, 91 and 120 end well yet are not squares.

Students will be able to infer what happens to the trailing zeros of a number when it is squared through observation and reasoning, and determine that squaring doubles the count of ending zeros, so a perfect square always ends in an even number of zeros. They will explain that a number ending in an odd count of zeros can never be a perfect square, and that squaring keeps parity, since an even number squares to even and an odd number squares to odd.

topics.summary: Every square is a running total of consecutive odd numbers, so subtracting those odds back off tests for a square and gives its root, and two consecutive triangular numbers always fit together into a square.

content.text: Add the odd numbers in order and the running totals are the perfect squares: 1, then 1 plus 3 is 4, then 1 plus 3 plus 5 is 9, and so on. The sum of the first k odd numbers is always k squared. The reason is that growing an n by n square into the next size adds an L-shaped strip of 2n plus 1 unit squares, which is the next odd number. The nth odd number itself is 2n minus 1. So instead of multiplying, you can step from one square to the next by adding the right odd number, for example 13 squared is 12 squared plus the 13th odd number, 144 plus 25, which is 169. Because consecutive squares differ by 2n plus 1, exactly 2n whole numbers lie strictly between n squared and (n plus 1) squared: between 12 squared, 144, and 13 squared, 169, there are 2 times 12, which is 24, whole numbers. A related pattern uses two consecutive numbers and their product: n squared plus (n plus 1) squared plus (n times (n plus 1)) squared equals (n times (n plus 1) plus 1) squared, so 6 squared plus 7 squared plus 42 squared is 43 squared.

content.text: Since every perfect square is the sum of consecutive odd numbers from 1, you can test a number by subtracting those same odd numbers back off. Take the number and subtract 1, then 3, then 5, and so on. If you land exactly on 0, the number is a perfect square, and the count of odd numbers you subtracted is its square root. If the running total jumps from a positive number straight past 0 without landing on it, the number is not a perfect square. For example, 121 reaches 0 after subtracting eleven odd numbers, so it is 11 squared, while 90 overshoots and is not a square.

media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Chapter 1 'A Square and A Cube', the square-root section. The class has built squares forwards and now has to run the same picture backwards, from the area to the side. Squaring, perfect squares and prime factorisation are assumed; the criterion vocabulary of estimation between consecutive squares is NOT - it is introduced here and is built from two multiplications every time it appears. Positive root only: this is the geometric reading and a side of minus eight is not a length, so no negative root is ever drawn or named. The words irrational, surd, non-terminating and approximation are not used, because this class has not met them.

overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Square fills the upper main panel, number line directly beneath it at full width, readouts to the right on a wide frame and collapsed into one strip under the line on a 390 px frame. The two markers are never drawn closer than 60 px apart; the line rescales instead. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not place the true side marker on the number line while a prediction is still open. The marker IS the answer.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.

overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Area is side times side, so recovering the side means undoing a multiplication by the same number, not undoing a doubling. Halving inverts adding a number to itself; rooting inverts multiplying a number by itself. The number line makes the difference concrete: at area 64 the half marker sits at 32 while the true side sits at 8, and the gap between them widens as the area grows. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with a square of area 64 and the side HIDDEN and asks whether the side is closer to 8 or to 32. Beat 2 drags the side until the area readout matches, and the two markers on the number line separate so the halving answer is seen to be far away. Beat 3 sets an area of 40, where no whole side works, and the tool names the two whole sides it falls between. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setArea, setSide, showHalfMarker and say.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on a square of area 64 with the side hidden and the line empty, and ask the class to commit closer to 8 or closer to 32, out loud. Commit the class answer. Target area 64. Never drag before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Set the side until the area readout reaches 64 and let the square turn green, then point at the half marker sitting at 32. Targets area 64, side 8, half marker 32. Read both numbers from the tool's own readouts. Call 3. Set the area to 40, let the handle refuse to snap, and name the two whole sides 6 and 7 that the true side lies between. Target area 40. Never round the side to a whole number.

media.description: One square stands on a countable unit grid above one number line of side lengths, the way a figure sits over a ruler. The square carries the area it really has printed inside it; the grid inside it is drawn at whole units so the side can be counted rather than guessed, and the unit is derived once per panel and then held constant across every area and every mode, so a bigger side is visibly bigger instead of being rescaled to fill the frame. Beneath, the number line runs from a drawn and labelled zero with arrowheads at both ends, ticks generated from the domain, and an italic caption reading side length. Two markers live on that one line at that one origin: the true side in the accent, with a pulsing dot and its value above the line, and the halving claim in the second accent, hollow and dashed, with its value and the words halving claims below the line - the claim is labelled as a claim about a LENGTH, never as half an area, so the tool does not model the very confusion of quantity it exists to break. When the area is a perfect square the handle settles on the whole side and the square fills green, which is the terminal moment of the search. When it is not, the tool refuses to snap and refuses to round: the square stays drawn at full strength, a shaded band appears between the two neighbouring whole sides with each end named, and the side is shown to three decimals with a trailing ellipsis and the plain statement that the digits go on and on. Beside the figure a two-line working strip prints the chapter's own line of working - the multiplication, then the drawn radical - and for a non-perfect area it prints the two multiplications that bracket it, so the bracket is built on screen rather than assumed as vocabulary the class has not met. The halving misconception is killed by construction rather than by assertion: the claimed side of 32 is drawn as its own dashed square of 1024 square units that runs clean off the top of the board.

Each item sets the target area from its own numbers, shows the question, then reveals the matching side, the number line and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with a square of area 64 and the side HIDDEN and asks whether the side is closer to 8 or to 32. Beat 2 drags the side until the area readout matches, and the two markers on the number line separate so the halving answer is seen to be far away. Beat 3 sets an area of 40, where no whole side works, and the tool names the two whole sides it falls between. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setArea, setSide, showHalfMarker and say.

concept.notation: Write the square root of a as root a. The root of a is the side of a square whose area is a, not half of a.
concept.statement: The square root of a number a is the side length of a square whose area is a. Halving gives a different number entirely, and the two only ever coincide at a equal to 4. When a is not a perfect square the side still exists, it simply is not a whole number, and it lies between the two nearest whole sides.
prerequisites: area of a square as side times side
misconceptions: Square root estimated as half of the number, so root 64 is taken as 32.
Believing a non perfect area has no side at all, rather than a side that is not whole.
concept.why_it_is_true: Area is side times side, so recovering the side means undoing a multiplication by the same number, not undoing a doubling. Halving inverts adding a number to itself; rooting inverts multiplying a number by itself. The number line makes the difference concrete: at area 64 the half marker sits at 32 while the true side sits at 8, and the gap between them widens as the area grows.
worked_numbers: Area 64: the side is 8, while half the area is 32, which is four times too big.
Area 40: no whole side works, and the side lies between 6 and 7 because 36 is 40 and 49 is not.
Area 4: the side is 2 and half the area is also 2, which is the single case where halving accidentally agrees.

answer_key.worked: The square root of an area is the side of the square that has that area. Halving the area gives a different number, and only area 4 makes the two agree.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn square: the exact side when the area is a perfect square, otherwise the pair of whole sides the true side lies between.
answer_key.precision: The side is held as a rational drag value and areas are compared with a tolerance of 0.001, but every graded value comes from exact integer work. A non integral root is shown to three decimals with a trailing ellipsis and the tool never claims the decimal ends.
answer_key.ground_truth: exactSide(a) = the integer s with s*s === a, found by integer search, or null. boundingPair(a) = [floor, floor+1] where floor is the largest integer f with f*f <= a, found by integer search. halfMarker(a) = a / 2, drawn only as the contrast marker and never graded as an answer.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The true side and the half marker land on the same point, which is the one case where halving is accidentally right. The tool says so plainly rather than hiding the case, because a rule that fails everywhere except one point is worth meeting.

The handle does not snap and the square does not turn green. The tool states that there is no whole number side and shows the nearest two whole sides, and it never rounds the side to make the picture close.
The side is 1 and the square is a single tile. Half the area is 0.5, which is drawn on the line below the smallest legal side, so the halving answer is not even a possible side.
Blocked before the operation with a stated reason on screen. A square of zero area is degenerate and a negative area is not a region, so the tool refuses rather than rendering a zero area figure.

edge_cases.case: A side dragged past the drawn range
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The drag clamps at 20 and the area readout stops with it. The tool says the handle has reached the end of the board rather than silently continuing to compute off screen.

teaching_notes: Beat 1 is the whole idea in one picture, and it is worth slowing down on the GRID rather than the number. The square of area 64 is drawn eight units on a side with eight columns and eight rows on screen, so a child can count the side instead of accepting it. Say the chapter's own line out loud as the strip prints it: area is side times side, so eight times eight is sixty-four, so the side is the square root of sixty-four. Ask the class to commit, out loud, whether the side is closer to 8 or to 32 BEFORE you land the beat, and commit their answer with predict('closer to 8') or predict('closer to 32'). The prediction is spoken; nothing on the screen asks for it.

Beat 2 is the argument, and the argument is a picture, not a sentence. Do not say halving is wrong and move on: point at the dashed square that the halving claim builds. A side of 32 draws a square of 1024 square units that does not fit on the board at all, beside a square of 64 that does. Then point at the two markers sitting on ONE line from ONE zero - 8 in the accent, 32 in the warm colour - and say that the second number is not a rough version of the first, it is a different number produced by a different rule. Halving undoes adding a number to itself; rooting undoes multiplying a number by itself.

Beat 3 is where the class will offer 6.5, and that is the moment to use. Six and a half times six and a half is 42.25, which overshoots 40, so the true side sits BELOW the midpoint of the bracket - the marker on screen is at 6.325 and you can see it sitting left of centre in the shaded band. Insist on the two statements being different: there is no WHOLE side, and there IS a side. The square of area 40 is drawn at full strength while the handle refuses to snap, precisely so refusing to snap cannot be read as refusing to exist. Say the ending in this grade's words - the digits go on and on and never stop - and do not reach for the word irrational.

media.title: Prime Factor Pairing
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash Chapter 1 'A Square and A Cube', square roots by prime factorisation. It follows the root as a side length: the student can already find a root by searching and now needs a method that says, without searching, whether a root exists at all. Everything is exact integer arithmetic — no decimal root anywhere — and the root is announced only as the product of one tile from each pair.

overview.goal: The student decides whether a number is a perfect square by pairing its prime factors, and states the smallest multiplier that makes it one.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground with a loose rail of prime factor tiles above a rebuild area. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A number is claimed not to be a perfect square, and the class is asked to say exactly what is stopping it.
overview.concept: A number is a perfect square exactly when every prime in its factorisation appears an even number of times, because the tiles can then be split into two identical halves and each half is the square root. A prime with an odd exponent leaves one tile unpaired, and the smallest multiplier that fixes it is the product of exactly those unpaired primes.
overview.purpose: The student decides whether a number is a perfect square by pairing its prime factors, and states the smallest multiplier that makes it one.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: Tile rail fills the main panel with the verdict strip beneath it and the multiply box under that. The factor tree, when shown, sits to the right on a wide frame and collapses above the rail on a 390 px frame. Draggable tiles are never placed closer than 60 px apart. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the verdict, the root or the smallest multiplier while a prediction is still open. The leftover tile IS the answer.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. If every prime appears an even number of times, the tiles split into two identical groups whose product is the same number s, so the original is s times s. If some prime appears an odd number of times, no such split exists, because one group would have to hold more copies of that prime than the other. The multiplier that repairs it must supply exactly one more copy of each odd prime, and nothing else, which is why it is the smallest. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with 180 broken into prime tiles, unpaired, and asks the class to decide whether it is a perfect square before anything is moved. Beat 2 pairs what pairs and leaves the single leftover tile red, so the obstruction is one visible object. Beat 3 multiplies by that leftover, rebuilds the factorisation, and the new number pairs completely. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setNumber, autoPair, multiplyBy and say. No drag: the agent cannot drag a tile with finite calls.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on 180 shown as loose prime tiles with nothing paired and no verdict, and ask the class to commit square or not a square, out loud. Commit the class verdict. Target the number 180. Never pair a tile before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Pair everything that pairs and leave the single 5 red and alone, then point at it. Targets the two 2s, the two 3s, and the lone 5. Read the factorisation from the tool's own tray. Call 3. Multiply by 5, let the factorisation rebuild, and read the root off one tile from each pair. Targets the multiplier 5, the rebuilt 900, and the root 30.

media.description: A number breaks into prime tiles on a loose rail, one tile per copy of each prime, drawn smallest prime first the way the Class 8 division ladder produces them. Two identical tiles lock together into a single green capsule; two unlike tiles refuse to join, shake apart and say why, so the rule is learnt from the refusal rather than from a red cross. A tile with no partner left anywhere stays outlined in red, which makes the obstruction one object the class can point at instead of a feeling that the number looks wrong. Above the rail the factorisation is typeset with real exponents, and beneath it, whenever every tile pairs, the two equal groups NCERT actually prints are written out as (2 × 3 × 5) × (2 × 3 × 5) with the root read off one of them. Multiplying rebuilds the factorisation as a fresh rail underneath the first, so a multiplier that only repairs half the problem visibly leaves a tile still red. A division ladder can be opened beside the rail. Concept walks 180 in three beats, Learn works the five reviewed checkpoints already answered, Practice serves six drawn questions on a difficulty ladder with a review pass, and Free Play unlocks the number box, the multiply box and free pairing with nothing scored.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the number from its own value, shows the question, then reveals the pairing, the leftover and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with 180 broken into prime tiles, unpaired, and asks the class to decide whether it is a perfect square before anything is moved. Beat 2 pairs what pairs and leaves the single leftover tile red, so the obstruction is one visible object. Beat 3 multiplies by that leftover, rebuilds the factorisation, and the new number pairs completely. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setNumber, autoPair, multiplyBy and say. No drag: the agent cannot drag a tile with finite calls.

concept.notation: Write the factorisation as a product of primes with exponents, for example 180 as 2 squared times 3 squared times 5. An exponent counts how many copies of that prime the number holds.
concept.statement: A number is a perfect square exactly when every prime in its factorisation appears an even number of times, because the tiles can then be split into two identical halves and each half is the square root. A prime with an odd exponent leaves one tile unpaired, and the smallest multiplier that fixes it is the product of exactly those unpaired primes.
prerequisites: prime factorisation and factor trees from Class 7
square numbers as n times n
misconceptions: Perfect square judged by appearance or by size rather than by the structure of its factors.
Square root treated as an operation with no factor meaning, so the pairing is copied as a procedure without the exponent link.
concept.why_it_is_true: If every prime appears an even number of times, the tiles split into two identical groups whose product is the same number s, so the original is s times s. If some prime appears an odd number of times, no such split exists, because one group would have to hold more copies of that prime than the other. The multiplier that repairs it must supply exactly one more copy of each odd prime, and nothing else, which is why it is the smallest.
worked_numbers: 180 is 2 squared times 3 squared times 5: the 5 is alone, so 180 is not a square and multiplying by 5 gives 900, which is 30 squared.
1225 is 5 squared times 7 squared: everything pairs, so it is a square and its root is 5 times 7, that is 35.
72 is 2 cubed times 3 squared: one 2 is alone, so multiplying by 2 gives 144, which is 12 squared.

answer_key.worked: A number is a perfect square exactly when every prime appears an even number of times. The smallest multiplier that makes it one is the product of the primes with odd exponents.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn tile set: whether every exponent is even, the root read off as one tile from each pair, or the product of the odd exponent primes.
answer_key.precision: Integer arithmetic only, with factorisation by trial division up to the integer square root. Exponents are held as a map from prime to count, never inferred from a decimal.
answer_key.ground_truth: factorise(k) = trial division by d from 2 while d*d <= k, returning a Map from prime to exponent. isSquare(k) = every exponent in factorise(k) is even. root(k) = product of p to the power e/2 over the map, computed only when isSquare(k). smallestMultiplier(k) = product of every prime whose exponent is odd.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The tile set is empty and every exponent is vacuously even, so 1 is a perfect square with root 1. The tool says so rather than treating an empty set as an error.

One tile, always unpaired, so it is never a square and the smallest multiplier is the prime itself. Worth showing because students expect primes to behave specially and here they behave in the simplest possible way.
The multiplier is the product of both, not either one alone. The tool refuses a multiplier that only fixes half the problem and shows which tile is still red.

edge_cases.case: A number that is already a perfect square
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The smallest multiplier is 1. The tool states that explicitly rather than leaving the box empty, because 1 is an answer and not an absence.

constraints: The multiset of prime tiles always multiplies back to the original number. A pairing move can never change the product, and a move that would is refused with the reason on screen.
Factorisation is by trial division up to the integer square root, with exponents stored as a map from prime to count.
The number is capped at 10 to the power 6 and the cap and its reason are stated on screen, so factorisation stays instant.
A pair may only contain two identical primes. A drag that would pair unlike tiles is refused and the tiles separate rather than being silently corrected.
The square root is announced only as the product of one tile from each pair, never computed by a floating point root, so the method and the answer stay the same object.

aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example factorising a number a child names and letting the class see which tile is left over.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
terminal_event.firedBy: the last item of the active bank being answered, or the student pressing Finish

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to put the whole factorisation of 180 on the table before anyone judges it. The class is asked out loud whether 180 is a perfect square while five loose tiles sit on the rail; the single 5 is already outlined in red, which is the evidence, not the verdict. Say the rule once here and let the tiles carry it.

Beat 2 is the argument in one motion. Everything that can pair locks into green capsules and exactly one tile is left alone, so 'not a square' stops being an opinion about how 180 looks and becomes a thing on screen with a colour and a position. Point at the red 5 and let a child name it.

Beat 3 turns the observation into an instrument. Multiplying by that same 5 rebuilds the rail as 900, every tile pairs, and the two equal groups (2 × 3 × 5) and (2 × 3 × 5) are written under it with the root 30 read off one of them — the NCERT justification, not a second trick.
media.generation_prompt: Prime Factor Pairing: a number breaks into prime factor tiles that the student drags into pairs, where paired tiles lock green and any leftover tile stays red until it is multiplied away
media.instructions_for_student: Tap two tiles that carry the same prime and they lock together as a pair; tap a locked pair to split it again. A tile with nobody left to pair with turns red, and those red tiles multiplied together are the smallest number you need to multiply by. When every tile is paired, the tiles split into two equal groups and each group multiplies to the square root.

media.title: Root Between Which Numbers
media.context: CBSE Class 8, NCERT Ganita Prakash chapter 1 'A Square and A Cube' (legacy NCERT chapter 6 'Squares and Square Roots'), the estimating-a-square-root section. It follows the prime-factor pairing tool: the class already knows when a whole root EXISTS and now needs a way to say something exact about the numbers where one does not. The chapter's own three-move procedure is what the tool draws - find the whole number whose square sits just below, state BOTH multiplications, then say which of the two the root is nearer by comparing the number with the two SQUARES. Vocabulary is held at grade: the input is labelled 'Number under the root', never 'radicand', and the words irrational, surd, bound, interval and strictly between appear nowhere on the glass.

overview.goal: The student places a non perfect square root between two consecutive whole numbers and names the two multiplications that prove both bounds.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A plain working ground carrying a single horizontal number line with the perfect squares labelled beneath it. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A root that is not a whole number still has to live somewhere, and the class is asked to say exactly where.
overview.concept: The square root of a number that is not a perfect square still exists and sits between the roots of the two nearest perfect squares. To prove root 55 lies between 7 and 8, both bounds are needed: 7 squared is 49 which is below 55, and 8 squared is 64 which is above it. One squaring alone traps nothing.
overview.purpose: The student places a non perfect square root between two consecutive whole numbers and names the two multiplications that prove both bounds.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: The line runs the full width of the main panel with the flag above it and the labels beneath. Readouts sit to the right on a wide frame and collapse to one strip under the line on a 390 px frame. The line never scrolls; it rescales. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not shade the interval or show either squaring while a prediction is still open. The shading IS the answer.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.

titleFraming.normal: Free Play · Root Between Which Numbers

overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Squaring keeps order for positive numbers: if a is less than b then a squared is less than b squared. So from 49 less than 55 less than 64 it follows that 7 is less than root 55 which is less than 8. The argument runs in both directions at once, which is why both squarings have to be named and not just the nearer one. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

learnMode.checkpointPlan: ML1 (Easy, Edge Case): The between two whole numbers question does not always have a between. Breaks: Believing every root needs two bounds. ML5 (Hard, Edge Case): One interval of length 1 on the root covers a widening run of radicands. Breaks: Believing each pair of bounds belongs to a single radicand.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the flag off the line and asks the class between which two whole numbers root 55 sits. Beat 2 drops the flag and shades the interval between the two nearest perfect squares. Beat 3 shows both squarings, 7 squared is 49 and 8 squared is 64, so the trap is closed from below and from above rather than asserted. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setRadicand, placeFlag, showBounds and say. No drag: the agent cannot sweep a continuous control with finite calls.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open with the flag off the line and nothing shaded, and ask the class to commit the two whole numbers the root sits between, out loud. Commit the class pair. Target the opening radicand. Never place the flag before the prediction is committed. Call 2. Drop the flag onto the line and shade the interval between the two nearest perfect squares, holding the committed guess beside it. Point at the shading. Read both bounds from the tool's own readouts. Call 3. Show the two multiplications beneath the shading, the square below the radicand and the square above it. Targets the lower square and the upper square. Never state a bound without the multiplication that proves it.

hunts: EXACT HUNT: find every radicand on the line whose root needs no interval at all.
OFF BY ONE: find a radicand one below a perfect square and say which bound it takes.
WIDEST RUN: find the pair of whole bounds that holds the most radicands on this line.
MAKE YOUR OWN: type any radicand in range, place the flag, then let the tool prove both bounds.

media.description: One horizontal number line runs across the frame carrying the ROOTS from 0 to 15, arrowheads at both ends, every whole number labelled beneath it and a flag standing above it. The number being rooted is an AREA, not a position, so it never appears loose under a tick: it is drawn as a typeset radical - a hand-built path with a real overbar - and, once the proof row opens, inside a middle plate that sits between the two multiplications, so the screen reads 7 x 7 = 49 < 55 < 8 x 8 = 64 in one line with a leader drawn from each square up to its own tick. The band between the two whole numbers shades above the line and closes from both sides at once. A zoom rescales the line to that one gap with tenth ticks and swaps the proof row for two bars drawn from ONE origin on ONE unit - 55 minus 49 is 6 against 64 minus 55 is 9 - which is how the class decides which of the two whole numbers the root is nearer without ever being told to halve the gap. Where the number IS a perfect square nothing shades at all: the flag lands on the marker and the tool says the root is whole rather than drawing a band that is not there. Learn walks five reviewed worked examples with the answer already on screen; Practice serves six of thirty reviewed questions on a difficulty ladder, hiding the band and both multiplications until the attempt is in; Free Play unlocks the number, the flag, the squares and the zoom with nothing scored.

mods.learn: Learn, teacher operated. The worked items arrive in props.learnQuestions, mandatory checkpoints first. Each item sets the radicand from its own number, shows the question, then reveals the shaded interval, both squarings and the answer together as one beat. Prev / Next move between items.
mods.ai_demo: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the flag off the line and asks the class between which two whole numbers root 55 sits. Beat 2 drops the flag and shades the interval between the two nearest perfect squares. Beat 3 shows both squarings, 7 squared is 49 and 8 squared is 64, so the trap is closed from below and from above rather than asserted. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setRadicand, placeFlag, showBounds and say. No drag: the agent cannot sweep a continuous control with finite calls.
mods.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own line. Give the bounding pair for a radicand, give a one decimal estimate, or name the two multiplications that prove the bounds. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer and the interval that settles it.
mods.free_play: Free Play, student operated. The student drags the flag anywhere, types any radicand, zooms into the shaded interval, and shows or hides the perfect square labels. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.

concept.notation: Write root 55 for the square root of 55. Saying it lies between 7 and 8 means 7 is below it and 8 is above it, both strictly.
concept.statement: The square root of a number that is not a perfect square still exists and sits between the roots of the two nearest perfect squares. To prove root 55 lies between 7 and 8, both bounds are needed: 7 squared is 49 which is below 55, and 8 squared is 64 which is above it. One squaring alone traps nothing.
prerequisites: square root as the side of a square of known area
reading and marking a number line
misconceptions: Roots must be whole numbers, so a non perfect radicand is treated as having no root.
Roots of non squares estimated by halving, or by rounding the radicand to the nearest square before rooting.
concept.why_it_is_true: Squaring keeps order for positive numbers: if a is less than b then a squared is less than b squared. So from 49 less than 55 less than 64 it follows that 7 is less than root 55 which is less than 8. The argument runs in both directions at once, which is why both squarings have to be named and not just the nearer one.
worked_numbers: Root 55 lies between 7 and 8, because 7 squared is 49 and 8 squared is 64.
Root 90 lies between 9 and 10, because 9 squared is 81 and 10 squared is 100.
Root 49 is exactly 7, so there is no interval to shade and the tool says so instead of shading a false one.
