answer_key.worked: Root 55 lies between 7 and 8, and the proof is the pair 7 squared is 49 and 8 squared is 64. Both squarings are part of the answer.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn line: the bounding pair for the radicand, the one decimal estimate within tolerance, or the two multiplications that prove the bounds.
answer_key.precision: Bounds are found by integer search, never by rounding a floating point root, so exact squares such as 10000 do not fall to the wrong side. A one decimal estimate is graded with a stated tolerance.
answer_key.ground_truth: lower(a) = the largest integer f with f*f <= a, found by integer search. upper(a) = lower(a) + 1 when a is not a perfect square, otherwise lower(a) itself. isExact(a) = lower(a)*lower(a) === a. estimate(a) = the one decimal value nearest root a, graded within a tolerance of 0.05.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.case: A radicand that is a perfect square

edge_cases.case: A radicand just below a perfect square
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The interval is still the full width between two whole numbers and the flag sits near its top. The tool never narrows the shading to suggest the root is almost whole.

edge_cases.case: A student naming only one bound
edge_cases.tool_behaviour: The stage stays open. One squaring traps nothing, so the tool asks for the second multiplication rather than accepting a half proof.
Bounds are found by integer search so the answer stays exact past the point where a floating point root would round the wrong way. The line rescales to the interval rather than the whole range.

constraints: Bounds are computed by integer search, never by rounding Math.sqrt, so a perfect square never falls to the wrong side of its own bound through floating point.
Once the answer is confirmed the flag cannot leave the interval implied by the correct bounds; a drag out of it is refused with the reason on screen.
A one decimal estimate is displayed with an explicit approximation marker and the tool never claims the expansion terminates.
The shaded interval is always the full span between two consecutive whole numbers, never narrowed towards the true root, because narrowing would give the answer away.
Both squarings are required to close the justification stage; naming one bound leaves the stage open with the missing side named.

steps: Predict: the line is drawn with the flag OFF it and no shading. The class commits the two whole numbers out loud and the teacher commits it on the pad. prediction_made unlocks the beat.

Prove it: 7 squared is 49 and 8 squared is 64 appear together beneath the shading, closing the trap from below and from above.

play_modes: EXACT HUNT: find every radicand on the line whose root needs no interval at all.
OFF BY ONE: find a radicand one below a perfect square and say which bound it takes.
WIDEST RUN: find the pair of whole bounds that holds the most radicands on this line.

normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. shared_state.note: Exactly what getState() returns and what rides every {type:'state'} emit. The teacher agent reads these field names, so they are a contract: renaming one silently breaks narration.

aiModeCalls.steps: next() / prev() / gotoStep(index) over the Concept beats; playDemo() auto runs them all
aiModeCalls.description: In Concept the agent orchestrates the demonstration from these calls. next() / prev() / gotoStep drive the 3 built in beats; the component calls let the agent branch a beat, for example trapping a radicand a child names and showing the two squarings that prove it.

postmessage.note: The tool emits {type:'ready', toolId} on mount and commands sent before it are DROPPED. Every windowMethod is also reachable as a command method.

agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

teaching_notes: Beat 1 exists to make the claim before the proof. The flag lands and the band shades, and the only thing on screen besides the line is the number itself, typeset under a radical. The class can already read the answer off the picture - which is exactly the position a student is in when they guess, and it is why beat 2 has something to do.

Beat 2 is the whole argument, and it is a two-sided one. 49 arrives from the left and 64 from the right and the row closes as 49 < 55 < 64, each square joined to its own tick by a drawn leader so nobody reads 49 as a position on a line that only goes to 15. Say the second multiplication out loud even when the class thinks the first settled it: with only 49 named, everything above 7 is still open.

Beat 3 turns the pair into an estimate and kills the halfway misconception in one picture. The line rescales to the one gap and the two bars - 6 against 9 - are drawn from the same origin on the same unit, so the class SEES that 55 sits nearer 49 than 64 and therefore the root sits nearer 7. Compare the number with the two SQUARES, never with the two whole numbers: that is the move students invert.
media.generation_prompt: Root Between Which Numbers: a number line from 0 to 15 with the perfect squares labelled underneath, where a dragged flag is trapped between the two squares that prove the bounds
media.instructions_for_student: A root that is not a whole number still lives somewhere on the line. Find the whole number whose square is just below your number, take the next one up, and the root sits between them. Say both multiplications - one alone proves nothing, because it leaves the root free on the other side. To judge which of the two it is nearer, compare your number with the two SQUARES, not with the two whole numbers. And if your number IS a perfect square, there is nothing to sit between: the root lands on a whole number.

media.title: Running the Square Machine Backwards
media.context: This hook opens the topic on square roots. Students know squares as areas. The film must not give either root, must not describe the prime factor method and must not state the trapping method.
media.description: You are told a square carpet covers a hundred and forty four square units of floor. How long is each side? Squaring took a side and gave an area, so now the machine has to run in reverse. Some areas give a clean whole side and others leave you stuck between two whole numbers.
media.teaching_notes: Learning objective: Find a square root exactly by prime factors, and trap it between whole numbers when it is not exact. Key teaching points: 1) A square root is the side of a square of the given area. 2) Pairing the prime factors finds an exact root. 3) If any prime is left unpaired, the root is not a whole number. 4) The answer can then be trapped between two consecutive whole numbers. Common misconceptions: 1) Students often halve the number instead of taking its root. 2) Students often give up when the root is not a whole number. Pause points: 0:23, at the end of one clean, one stuck: ask what the side of the first carpet must be. 0:23, just before the open question: ask which two whole numbers trap the second. Questions to ask: before viewing, ask what taking a square root undoes. After viewing, ask how prime factors could help.

topics.summary: A square root is the side of a square of that area, and every perfect square has a positive and a negative integer root. Pairing prime factors gives an exact root, and trapping a non-square between neighbouring squares estimates its root.

content.text: If a square has area A, its side is the square root of A, written with the root symbol. The square root of a number is the value that, multiplied by itself, gives that number. So the square root of 144 is 12, because 12 times 12 is 144. Undoing a square this way is the inverse of squaring. Every perfect square actually has two integer square roots, because a negative number times itself is also positive: both 12 and minus 12 square to 144. When the root stands for a length, such as the side of a square, we use only the positive one.

So the square root of 144 is 12, because 12 times 12 is 144. Undoing a square this way is the inverse of squaring. Every perfect square actually has two integer square roots, because a negative number times itself is also positive: both 12 and minus 12 square to 144. When the root stands for a length, such as the side of a square, we use only the positive one.

content.text: Break a number into its prime factors. A perfect square has each prime appearing an even number of times, so the primes can be split into two identical groups. Taking one prime from each pair rebuilds one of those groups, and that product is the square root. For example, 784 is 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 7 x 7, so its root is 2 x 2 x 7, which is 28. If some prime is left without a partner, the number is not a perfect square. To make such a number into a square, multiply by the smallest value that gives each unpaired prime a partner. For instance, 588 is 2 x 2 x 3 x 7 x 7 with a lone 3, so multiplying by 3 gives 1764, whose root is 42. When you need the smallest square divisible by several numbers, first take their LCM so the result is a multiple of all of them, then supply the missing prime partners. For example, the smallest square divisible by 6, 8 and 15 starts from their LCM 120, which is 2 x 2 x 2 x 3 x 5, and multiplying by 2 x 3 x 5 gives 3600, a perfect square with root 60.

content.text: When a number is not a perfect square, you can still estimate its root by trapping it between the two nearest perfect squares. Since roots grow in the same order as the numbers, the root lies between the roots of those two squares. For example, 200 lies between 196 and 225, so its root is between 14 and 15, and because 200 is closer to 196, the root is nearer 14. Comparing the number with the two squares tells you which whole number the root is closest to. To find the largest whole-number side of a square that fits inside a given area, take the root of the largest perfect square that does not exceed the area.

learning_objectives.objective_text: Students will be able to infer what the side of a square of given area represents through observation and reasoning, and determine that the square root of A is the value which multiplied by itself gives A, so the square root of 144 is 12 and taking a root undoes squaring. They will explain that every perfect square has two integer roots, one positive and one negative, since a negative times itself is positive, but only the positive root is used when it stands for a length.
Examine the worked examples of the square root is the side of the square, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving the square root is the side of the square, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what the prime factors of a perfect square reveal through observation and reasoning, and determine that each prime appears an even number of times, so taking one prime from each pair rebuilds the square root, as 784 is 2 x 2 x 2 x 2 x 7 x 7 with root 2 x 2 x 7 which is 28. They will explain that a lone unpaired prime means the number is not a perfect square, and that multiplying by the smallest value which gives every unpaired prime a partner turns it into a square, so 588 times 3 is 1764 with root 42.
Examine the worked examples of square roots by pairing prime factors, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving square roots by pairing prime factors, across different cases.

Students will be able to infer what the two nearest perfect squares tell them about a root through observation and reasoning, and determine that a root lies between the roots of the squares that trap the number, so the root of 200 lies between 14 and 15 because 200 lies between 196 and 225. They will explain that comparing the number with those two squares shows which whole number the root is nearest, so the root of 200 is nearer 14 since 200 is closer to 196.
Examine the worked examples of estimating a square root by trapping it, across different cases.
Examine the practised examples and practice questions involving estimating a square root by trapping it, across different cases.

media.title: Cube Stacker
media.context: CBSE Class 8, Ganita Prakash Ch.1 'A Square and A Cube', the cube half of the chapter. The class has the square array in hand and volume as a count of unit cubes from Class 7; neither is re-taught. Cube roots by prime factorisation come LATER in the same chapter, so the tool never writes the radical sign and asks 'what is its side?' in words instead. It is read at the Build beat of the topic 'Cubes and Their Digits' and rehearses the 1-mark cube-count reading and the 2-mark reverse item directly.

finish.normal: The same panel with no star and evaluated false. There is no play again loop.
finish.practice: A full screen celebration carrying a star rating from the real score, all correct 3, 60 per cent or more 2, else 1 and never 0, plus a what you have learned panel and Review. The star screen offers Review, which walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer, and the layered stack that explains it.
whatYouLearned: A cube of side n holds n times n times n unit cubes
Each layer holds n squared, and there are n layers
Cubing is never multiplying by three, at any whole side

overview.goal: The student builds an n cubed stack in a flat drawing and states the number of unit cubes without counting them one by one.
overview.theme: Class 8 register: clean geometric line work, one accent plus one second accent, no decoration Setting: A flat working surface drawn in a fixed oblique view, the way a stack of dice sits on a table. Character: none, because this mount is an instrument. Premise: A class says a cube of side four needs twelve small cubes, and the stack itself is asked to settle it.
overview.concept: A cube of side n is built from n layers, each of which is an n by n square holding n squared unit cubes. The total is therefore n squared taken n times, that is n times n times n, written n cubed. Multiplying by three would give three copies of a length, which is not a solid at all.
overview.purpose: The student builds an n cubed stack in a flat drawing and states the number of unit cubes without counting them one by one.
overview.blackboard: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order. Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
overview.uiOverview: The stack fills the main panel with the three readouts in a single row directly beneath it. Add layer and remove layer sit as large buttons below the readouts on a 390 px frame and to the right on a wide frame. Every button keeps a 44 px hit target. The Finish button renders ONLY in Practice and Free Play, gated positively on the mode. The HOST renders the mode selector, the language switcher and the mute in its own bar; this tool does not draw them and never lists the mode selector as a student control.
overview.neverRemove: Do not show the total while a prediction is still open, and never draw a layer that is not n by n. The total IS the answer and a non square layer is a lie about the solid.
overview.predictFirst: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
overview.flowOfUnderstanding: Predict, then observe, then compare, then conclude. Each layer is a square of side n and so holds n squared cubes, and there are n such layers stacked to make the height n. Adding n squared to itself n times is n times n squared, which is n cubed. The three readouts are kept separate precisely so that the layer count and the cubes per layer never blur into one number. Concept reveals the idea in 3 beats, Learn works the five checkpoints solved, Practice serves six drawn questions scored, and Free Play unlocks everything with nothing required.

conceptMode.summary: Concept, agent driven, 3 teaching beats. Beat 1 opens with the ghost outline of a side 4 cube, nothing built and the total HIDDEN, and asks the class how many small cubes it will need. Beat 2 adds the layers one at a time, each completed layer flashing, with the layer count and the cubes per layer moving separately. Beat 3 hides the total and asks why it is side times side times side rather than side times three, pointing at the layer readout as the evidence. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setSide, addLayer, highlightLayer and say.

conceptMode.teacherCallPlan: Call 1. Open on the ghost outline of a side 4 cube with nothing built and the total hidden, and ask the class to predict the cube count out loud. Commit the class number. Target side 4. Never build before the prediction is committed, and never say 64 at this call. Call 2. Build the four layers one at a time and point at the three readouts as they move. Targets side 4, four layers, 16 cubes per layer. Read the total from the tool's own readout. Call 3. Hide the total again and ask why it is side times side times side rather than side times three, pointing at the layer readout as the evidence. Target the layer that shows 16.

hunts: EQUAL COUNT HUNT: find a square and a cube that hold the same number of units.
TRIPLING HUNT: look for a side where cubing and tripling agree, and say why the search ends empty.
BETWEEN CUBES: pick a total that is not a cube and name the two sides it falls between.
BUILD YOUR OWN: choose any side, predict the total, then build it layer by layer and check.

media.description: A ghost outline of the finished cube stands on a flat working surface in a fixed oblique view, drawn with the unit grid on its three visible faces so the target can be counted before a single cube is placed. Layers of n by n unit cubes then drop into it one at a time, each flashing once in the second accent as it lands, while three separate read-outs move independently: the layer count, the cubes per layer (which does not move at all while layers are added) and the running total. Keeping those three apart is the whole design, because the misconception the tool exists to break is the two factors blurring into one and the raised 3 being read as a multiplier. Concept builds a side-4 cube, rebuilds it layer by layer so the total is seen jumping by a whole 16, and then places only 12 cubes inside the same outline so that 4 x 3 = 12 is visibly three quarters of ONE layer rather than a solid. Learn walks the five reviewed checkpoints, each opening with its own scene and its answer already on screen: one unit cube at side 1, a side-2 stack beside a flat row of 6, a side-2 stack beside the 4 cubes left over from a tray of 12, the full 216 at the draw cap, and a side-4 stack beside a flat 8 by 8 array so both counts land on 64. Practice serves six of the thirty reviewed questions on a difficulty ladder that climbs on a correct answer and drops on a wrong one, with the ghost outline drawn and the total withheld until an attempt is in, and any cube above the side-6 cap drawn as a labelled wireframe so the rule can outlive the picture. Free Play unlocks the side selector, both layer buttons and the outline toggle with nothing scored.

Beat 2 adds the layers one at a time, each completed layer flashing, with the layer count and the cubes per layer moving separately. Beat 3 hides the total and asks why it is side times side times side rather than side times three, pointing at the layer readout as the evidence. The agent advances with next() / prev() / gotoStep and can compose a beat with setSide, addLayer, highlightLayer and say.
mods.practice: Practice, student operated. The bank from props.questions, one item at a time, each rendering its own stack. Give the cube count for a stated side, judge whether a number is a perfect cube, or give the side for a stated count. Scored, with a star finish and a Review phase that walks every item showing the student's answer, the correct answer and the stack that settles it.
mods.free_play: Free Play, student operated. The student sets the side, adds and removes layers freely, shows or hides the ghost outline, and reads the three counts at any point in the build. Nothing is scored and nothing is mandatory.

scenes.interaction: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. concept.notation: Write n cubed, read as 'n cubed' or 'n to the power 3'. The raised 3 counts how many factors of n are multiplied, it is not a multiplier.
concept.statement: A cube of side n is built from n layers, each of which is an n by n square holding n squared unit cubes. The total is therefore n squared taken n times, that is n times n times n, written n cubed. Multiplying by three would give three copies of a length, which is not a solid at all.
prerequisites: square numbers as an n by n array
volume as a count of unit cubes from Class 7
misconceptions: Cubing read as multiplying by three, so 4 cubed is taken as 12.
Confusion of the exponent with a multiplier, so the raised 3 is read as 'times 3'.
concept.why_it_is_true: Each layer is a square of side n and so holds n squared cubes, and there are n such layers stacked to make the height n. Adding n squared to itself n times is n times n squared, which is n cubed. The three readouts are kept separate precisely so that the layer count and the cubes per layer never blur into one number.
worked_numbers: Side 3: three layers of nine, so 27 cubes; multiplying by three would have said 9.
Side 4: four layers of sixteen, so 64 cubes, and the doubling of the side from 2 to 4 multiplies the total by eight, not by two.
Side 6: six layers of thirty six, so 216 cubes, which is the largest stack the tool draws.

setSideOutcomes.1: one cube, the smallest legal stack

answer_key.worked: A cube of side n is n layers of n squared unit cubes, so it holds n times n times n, written n cubed.
answer_key.practice: Computed per item at runtime from the drawn stack: the total for the stated side, whether the stated number is a perfect cube, or the side for a stated total.
answer_key.precision: Integer arithmetic only. Totals are exact integer products and cube tests are done by integer search, never by a floating point cube root.
answer_key.ground_truth: total(n) = n * n * n, computed as an integer product. cubesPerLayer(n) = n * n. isPerfectCube(k) = integer search for r in 0..k with r*r*r === k. cubeRoot(k) = that r, or null when none exists.

blackboard.rule: Any theorem, derivation, proof, formula or numerical calculation that takes MORE THAN TWO mathematical steps is written on the blackboard step by step, one step below the previous one, in logical order.

modes.ai: The agent narrates while the board fills; the board never runs ahead of the narration.
modes.learn: The board is the reveal. Before reveal() it is empty; on reveal it fills line by line, then the answer lands last.
modes.normal: No board unless the student asks the tool to settle something, then the same line by line fill.
modes.practice: The board stays empty until the answer is checked, then fills line by line as the explanation.

blackboard.for_a_proof: State the claim first, then write and explain each step in sequence, then close on the conclusion.
blackboard.readability: Keep the board clean and uncrowded, at Class 8 reading level, with the same symbols the scene uses.
blackboard.applies_when: The explanation runs to more than two mathematical steps. Two steps or fewer may be written together.
blackboard.for_a_calculation: Show the complete working line by line, including every intermediate value, before the final answer is shown.
blackboard.one_step_per_line: Never show all the steps at once and never combine two calculations into one line. One calculation per line.
blackboard.source_of_the_lines: The `steps` array of the Learn checkpoint or Practice question on screen IS the blackboard, in order. Render one array entry per line. It is gated at build time: no entry carries two calculations.
blackboard.builds_progressively: The board fills line by line as the explanation is given, so the student can see how each step follows from the one above it. A line already written stays on the board.

edge_cases.tool_behaviour: One layer of one cube. It is a legal cube and the smallest one, and the three readouts all read 1, which shows the student that cubing leaves 1 unmoved.

The three readouts stay honest: the layer count is what has been built, the cubes per layer is n squared, and the total is what is on screen, not the finished total. The ghost outline shows the target separately.
The stack returns to empty with the ghost outline still present. Empty is a legal state and the tool renders it rather than snapping back to one layer.

constraints: Layers are always n by n. The stack can never become a cuboid, and a move that would make one is refused with the reason on screen.
The drawing is a fixed two dimensional oblique projection. There is no 3D engine and no free rotation.
The oblique offset per depth level is precomputed and the faces are drawn back to front so overlap is correct; the depth ordering is recomputed only when n changes.
At most 216 unit faces are rendered. Above that the stack is drawn as a labelled outline rather than as individual cubes.
The three readouts are separate state fields and are never derived from one another at render time, so a partly built stack cannot report a finished total.

play_modes: EQUAL COUNT HUNT: find a square and a cube that hold the same number of units.
TRIPLING HUNT: look for a side where cubing and tripling agree, and say why the search ends empty.
BETWEEN CUBES: pick a total that is not a cube and name the two sides it falls between.
BUILD YOUR OWN: choose any side, predict the total, then build it layer by layer and check.
normal.parameter_freedom: Every adjustable parameter is unlocked inside its invariant limits, nothing is scored, nothing progresses, and no question is posed. The student sets the values, and may pose their own question and let the tool settle it, because the tool keeps computing and showing its invariants the whole time. agent_control.operator_note: Concept (ai) and Learn are TEACHER operated. The agent calls the step verbs and narrates; the class watches and answers out loud. No beat in these two modes may carry operate-the-control copy (no 'tap your guess', 'press Check', 'drag the marker'). Keep the thinking half of the sentence ('Predict first', 'Say your answer out loud first') and drop the device half. Practice and Free Play are student operated and address the student directly.

predict_first.rule: Step 1 of every mode that teaches opens with the CONTENT HIDDEN. The student commits a prediction before the tool shows any result, marked answer, filled table or read out. Committing emits prediction_made, which unlocks step 1 so the real result animates in BESIDE the guess.
predict_first.scope: Step 1 only. Steps 2..N use the ordinary reveal gate: scene and question shown, answer hidden until reveal.
mechanism: a prediction state field on the shared state
a predict verb in windowMethods
a prediction_made event listed in events[]
the emit fires once per step 1, never re-asked on later steps

terminal_event.name: finished
terminal_event.note: The host treats name === 'completed' || name === 'finished' as end of activity and writes the lesson summary. Emit 'finished' exactly once, guarded by a one shot ref that only reset() re-arms; the celebration overlay and chime sit OUTSIDE the guard so a second tap re-opens them. Never emit a bare 'completed', and never name a progress event '*_completed'. Progress events are named for what happened (step_done, example_done, bank_done). The Finish button renders ONLY in practice and normal, gated on the MODE, never on operatorMode.
